title: Vendor Safety Requirements
summary: Free induction for vendors, suppliers and delivery drivers visiting Shell Mobility Oman sites: site rules, work at height and access, documents to carry, lifting and offloading, and PPE.

lessons.title: Basics: arriving and moving on site
body: Every vendor visit to a Shell Mobility site in Oman starts the same way. Arrive during working hours, report to the Site Supervisor or Station Manager first, and get your site safety induction before you do anything else. From then on, the site or station manager's instructions apply to you.

Drive slowly and predictably. Follow the posted site speed limit (10 km/h on retail forecourts), never drive against the traffic flow, and never reverse a vehicle without a signalman guiding you. Park only in the designated areas so emergency routes and fuel delivery bays stay clear.

Know the site Emergency Response Plan (ERP): where the emergency stops, extinguishers and assembly point are. Smoking is only allowed in designated areas on construction sites and is never allowed on a retail station.
keyPoints: Report to the Site Supervisor or Station Manager and get inducted FIRST.
Follow the 10 km/h speed limit and never reverse without a signalman.
Know the site ERP and assembly point.
No smoking anywhere on a retail station.

images.caption: HSSE Guidance for Vendors — Basics, Work at Height & Access

quiz.prompt: What must you do before starting any activity on site?
quiz.explanation: The site safety induction always comes first, after reporting to the Site Supervisor or Station Manager.

quiz.prompt: When may you reverse a vehicle on site?
options: Only with a signalman guiding you
quiz.explanation: No reversing without a signalman.

quiz.prompt: Where may you smoke at a retail fuel station?
options: In a designated area away from pumps
Nowhere — no smoking on retail stations
quiz.explanation: Smoking is not allowed on retail stations; only in designated areas on construction sites.

lessons.title: Work at height and access
body: Falls from vehicles and platforms are one of the most common ways vendors get hurt. Do not climb onto any platform or vehicle bed higher than 4 ft (120 cm) without safe access, and never jump down from one.

Any access above 1.8 metres needs a permit. To fix lifting gear at height, use a ladder that someone else is holding at the base. Inspect the ladder before use, keep three points of contact, always face the ladder while climbing up or down, and never over-reach.
Be aware of overhead power lines and moving traffic, and barricade your work area so customers and vehicles stay out.
keyPoints: No climbing above 120 cm without safe access — and no jumping down.
Above 1.8 m you need a permit.
Ladders: inspected, footed by a second person, 3-point contact, face the ladder.
Barricade your work area.

quiz.prompt: Above what height does access require a permit?
quiz.explanation: Access to more than 1.8 metres requires a permit.

quiz.prompt: How should you climb a ladder?
options: Facing away, carrying tools in both hands
Quickly, two rungs at a time
Leaning out to reach the work
quiz.explanation: Always face the ladder and keep three points of contact.

quiz.prompt: You need to fix a lifting gear at height. What is correct?
options: Stand on the vehicle's side rail
Use a ladder secured by another person at the base
quiz.explanation: Use a ladder that is footed by another person.

lessons.title: Documents you must carry
body: Before work or a delivery can start, the site needs to see the right paperwork. For deliveries: the delivery challan and the Safety Data Sheets for any chemicals. On arrival, make the daily site log entry, show your Safety Passport / site induction record, and be ready for a breathalyser test.
For work activities you also need the method statement (methodology) and a Work Clearance Form.

For lifting: third-party certificates for all lifting and hoisting components, the operator's licence and/or third-party competency certificate, a physical fitness certificate for the operator on critical lifts, a lifting plan that matches the lift category, and a Job Hazard Analysis plus a permit for critical lifts.
keyPoints: Delivery challan and Safety Data Sheets.
Daily site log, Safety Passport, breathalyser test.
Method statement and Work Clearance Form.
Lifting: 3rd-party certificates, operator licence, lift plan, JHA and permit for critical lifts.

images.caption: HSSE Guidance for Vendors — Documentation, Lifting / Offloading

quiz.prompt: Which document tells the site what hazardous chemicals you are bringing?
quiz.explanation: Safety Data Sheets describe the hazards of each chemical.

quiz.prompt: What is needed for every lifting and hoisting component?
quiz.explanation: All lifting and hoisting components need valid third-party certificates.

quiz.prompt: Which test may you be asked to take on arrival?
quiz.explanation: Breathalyser tests are done at site.

lessons.title: Lifting, offloading and PPE
body: Your vehicle must be fit for use, and anyone operating a crane must hold valid training and a licence for it. Critical lifts need a permit; minor lifts need at least a JHA or Work Clearance Form. Stay out of the line of fire of any load, and use safe manual handling techniques when lifting by hand.
Wear the right PPE at all times on site: hard hat, high-visibility vest, safety shoes, protective clothing (coverall), gloves and goggles. Work safe, home safe.
keyPoints: Critical lifts: permit. Minor lifts: JHA or WCF.
Crane operators need valid training and licence.
Stay out of the line of fire.
PPE: hard hat, hi-viz, safety shoes, coverall, gloves, goggles.

quiz.prompt: What is needed for a minor lift?
options: A JHA or Work Clearance Form
A full permit and lift plan approved by Shell Engineering
quiz.explanation: Use a permit for critical lifts and a JHA or WCF for minor lifts.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT part of the required PPE list?
quiz.explanation: Safety shoes are required — never sandals.

quiz.prompt: Where should you stand during offloading by crane?
options: Under the load to guide it
Away from the line of fire
quiz.explanation: Position yourself away from the line of fire.

title: Riggers and Banksmen
summary: For supervisors who plan and control lifting and rigging at Shell Mobility sites: roles, rigging fundamentals, load weight, crane capacity, sling angles, exclusion zones and the IOGP 376 lift categories, with the Start-Work Checks.

lessons.title: The Lifting Supervisor's role and precautions
body: Most lifting accidents trace back to a short list of failures: no risk assessment, controls from the risk assessment not implemented, no proper lifting plan, no permit to work to manage the lift, wrong rigging methods, poorly maintained lifting equipment, and poor site control — no exclusion zone, so people not involved in the lift walk into it.

The Lifting Supervisor coordinates and supervises every lift in line with the Lifting Plan. Before work starts they brief the whole lifting team — crane operator, riggers and signalmen — on the plan, the risk controls and the safe lifting procedure; make sure only registered crane operators and appointed riggers and signalmen take part; check the ground is safe for mobile cranes; and stay present for the whole lift, putting right any unsafe condition reported to them.

General precautions on our sites: hold a toolbox talk, have the risk assessment and method statement on hand, keep phones away during the lift, check third-party inspection certificates, and agree the communication method. Terminate work above 45 °C, at wind speeds of 20 knots or more, or above 80% humidity, and never lift when visibility is poor. Provide one First Aider and one Fire Warden per 25 workers.
PPE for every member of the lifting team: safety helmet, high-visibility vest, coverall, safety boots, gloves, and eye and hearing protection.
keyPoints: The Lifting Supervisor briefs the team and is present for the whole lift.
Only registered operators and appointed riggers/signalmen.
Stop work above 45 °C, at 20 knots wind, above 80% humidity or in poor visibility.
1 First Aider + 1 Fire Warden per 25 workers.

quiz.prompt: Which wind speed should stop lifting work on our sites?
quiz.explanation: Work is terminated at 20 knots.

quiz.prompt: Who must be present for the entire lifting operation?
quiz.explanation: The Lifting Supervisor must be present during all lifting operations.

quiz.prompt: What is a common root cause of lifting accidents?
quiz.explanation: Absence or lack of a proper Lifting Plan is a frequent cause.

quiz.prompt: How many First Aiders and Fire Wardens are needed for 25 workers?
quiz.explanation: One First Aider and one Fire Warden per 25 employees.

lessons.title: Rigging fundamentals: WLL, design factor and hitches
body: Overhead lifting is any lift that raises a freely suspended load to a position where dropping it could injure someone or damage property.

The Working Load Limit (WLL) is the maximum load that may be applied in direct tension to an undamaged, straight length of sling or hoisting equipment. It is always less than the breaking strength. The design factor is the ratio of breaking strength to WLL: a chain sling with a breaking strength of 100 and a WLL of 25 has a design factor of 4:1.
Minimum design factors: alloy steel chain sling 4:1; wire rope, nylon rope, polypropylene rope, metal mesh, synthetic web and synthetic round slings 5:1; polyester rope sling 7:1.

Reach is measured from the top of the master link to the bowl of the load hook. Use a single master link for single and two-legged chain slings, and a master link with sub-links for three- or four-legged slings. The three basic hitches are vertical, choker and basket — each changes the sling's capacity, so always read the sling tag for the hitch you are using.

Sling choice: alloy chain is durable, repairable and tolerant of heat but heavy; wire rope is cheaper and lighter but hard to inspect, kinks easily and cannot be repaired; metal mesh resists cuts and abrasion but any broken wire removes it from service; synthetic slings are light and protect the load but are damaged by heat (about 90 °C / 194 °F), cuts, chemicals and UV and cannot be repaired.
keyPoints: WLL is always less than the breaking strength.
Design factor = breaking strength ÷ WLL (chain 4:1, most slings 5:1, polyester rope 7:1).
Basic hitches: vertical, choker, basket.
Synthetic slings cannot be repaired and fail with heat, cuts and chemicals.

quiz.prompt: The WLL of rigging equipment is …
quiz.explanation: WLL is a fraction of the breaking strength.

quiz.prompt: What is the minimum design factor of an alloy steel chain sling?
quiz.explanation: Alloy steel chain slings are 4:1.

quiz.prompt: A sling has a breaking strength of 10 t and a design factor of 5:1. What is its WLL?
Which sling type cannot be repaired and is damaged by heat and UV?
quiz.explanation: Synthetic slings have low heat resistance, suffer from UV and chemicals, and cannot be repaired.

lessons.title: Load weight, crane capacity and sling angles
body: Know how heavy the load is. Take the actual weight from engineering data, shipping papers or catalogues, or calculate it from the volume of the object and the weight of the material (reduced for any voids). Always add the weight of the rigging and hardware.

Crane capacity comes from the manufacturer's load chart. It depends on the load radius (horizontal distance from the centre of rotation to the centre of the load), the boom length including jib or extensions, the boom angle, and the weight of attachments and handling devices such as the hook block and rigging. Mistakes here tip cranes over — overloads, side loading and loads swinging outside the radius in wind have all overturned cranes.

Sling angle changes the load in each leg. The Sling Angle Factor (SAF) for the angle from horizontal is: 90° = 1.000, 60° = 1.155, 45° = 1.415, 30° = 2.000. Multiply the share of the load on each leg by the SAF. Avoid shallow angles by using longer slings or a spreader beam, and protect slings from sharp edges.

Capture the centre of gravity: a suspended load always settles with its CoG under the hook, so place the lift point above the CoG, not the middle of the object, and do a test lift to confirm stability.
keyPoints: Load weight includes rigging and hardware.
Capacity depends on radius, boom length, boom angle and attachments.
Lift above the centre of gravity and do a test lift.

resources.label: Video: How to calculate the weight of a load (Drive)

quiz.prompt: What must be included in the load weight?
options: The object plus rigging and hardware
quiz.explanation: Include the weight of rigging equipment and hardware.

quiz.prompt: What is the sling angle factor at 30° from horizontal?
quiz.explanation: At 30° the tension in each leg doubles: SAF 2.000.

quiz.prompt: A 2 t load hangs on two legs at 60°. What is the tension in each leg?
quiz.explanation: Each leg takes 1 t × 1.155 = 1.155 t.

quiz.prompt: Where should the lift point be?
options: Directly above the centre of gravity
quiz.explanation: Centre the lift above the centre of gravity.

lessons.title: Exclusion zones, power lines, weather and landing
body: Barricade the full swing radius of the crane and keep everyone not involved out of the lift area. Nobody walks or stands under a suspended load — that is a Life-Saving Rule. Make sure the operator can see clearly (no broken or obstructed windows) and keep loads as close to the ground as possible.

Overhead power lines: know their location and voltage and agree precautions with the owner. Minimum exclusion zones: low-voltage lines 1 m; 11 kV and 33 kV 3 m; 132 kV 6 m; 275 kV and 400 kV 7 m. Increase the distance in wet conditions.

Weather: wind makes loads swing — use tag lines unless they create a greater hazard. Heat reduces sling WLL: synthetic slings are affected above about 90 °C, wire rope above 150 °C and chain above 200 °C. Consider rain, visibility and ground: level, dry and stable, with outriggers fully extended on mats.

Flying and landing: have a clear path from pick-up to landing, never fly the load over people, move smoothly and avoid sudden starts and stops. Plan the landing before you lift, land on a firm flat surface on blocks or cribbing — never on the slings — chock round loads, and slowly release tension.

Before work starts, the Start-Work Checks for lifting and rigging must all be confirmed: written lift plan (if required) agreed by everyone; operator and rigger qualified; load within the equipment's safe working limit; lifting and rigging gear certified, inspected and rated; safety devices in place and working; communication plan agreed; controls for load shift, dropped objects, obstructions, power lines and suspended loads; and lifting equipment stable per the manufacturer. If any is missing — stop and seek help.
keyPoints: Barricade the swing radius; never stand under a suspended load.
Power line clearance: LV 1 m, 11/33 kV 3 m, 132 kV 6 m, 275/400 kV 7 m.
Land on blocks or cribbing — never on the slings.
All 8 Start-Work Checks must be confirmed before lifting.

quiz.prompt: Minimum exclusion distance from a 132 kV overhead line?
quiz.explanation: 132 kV lines need 6 m.

quiz.prompt: How should a load be landed?
options: On blocks or cribbing so slings can be removed
quiz.explanation: Never land a load directly on the slings.

quiz.prompt: One Start-Work Check cannot be confirmed. What do you do?
options: Ask the operator to be careful
Skip it if the lift is short
quiz.explanation: Stop and seek help if any safeguard is not in place.

quiz.prompt: When should tag lines be used?
options: Always, unless their use creates an unsafe condition
quiz.explanation: Tag lines shall be used unless their use creates an unsafe condition.

lessons.title: Lift categories and key controls (IOGP 376)
body: Shell Mobility's Lifting & Hoisting guideline (04.100) follows IOGP Report 376. A Person in Charge is appointed for every lift and categorises it; a Lift Plan is required for every lift regardless of category; everyone involved must be trained and competent; lifting equipment is visually inspected before and after each use and thoroughly examined by an independent competent inspector; and a banksman / signaller assists the crane operator.

Work through the categories from the top. Category 3 (non-routine complex) if any apply: load over 90% of the crane's rated capacity at that radius; lifting people; tandem lifts; proximity hazards such as power lines or confined spaces; lifting over live plant; more than one shift; needs expert calculations; transfer between appliances; blind lifts; rotating or up-ending the load. Category 3 should be avoided and needs Shell Engineering deviation approval with a qualified-person review of the Lift Plan.

Category 2 (non-routine simple) if any apply: load over 80% of the rated capacity; outside normal operating conditions; uneven or shifting weight; restrictive weather; unusual shape; estimated weight; sharp edges; no designed lifting points; excessive dimensions; SIMOPS. Category 1 (routine) only when none of the above apply, the people are trained, competent and authorised, and the load and equipment are simple.

Typical retail work: underground tank installation, canopy erection, monolith and HRS installation and site cabins are usually Category 2; steel structures, charger and dispenser installation, substations and deliveries are usually Category 1. Critical lifts by crane and lifts over 5,000 kg are high-risk work that needs a permit.
keyPoints: A Lift Plan is required for every lift.
Category 3 (>90% capacity, people, tandem, power lines, blind lifts…) should be avoided.
Category 2 starts above 80% capacity or with estimated weight, uneven load, unusual shape.
Critical crane lifts and lifts over 5,000 kg need a permit.

quiz.prompt: A crane will lift a load at 85% of its rated capacity at that radius. Which category, at minimum?
quiz.explanation: Over 80% (but not over 90%) is Category 2.

quiz.prompt: Which lift is Category 3?
options: A routine dispenser delivery by forklift
Lifting a person in a basket
A load of known weight at 50% capacity
A lift with designed lifting points
quiz.explanation: Lifting or lowering personnel is always Category 3.

quiz.prompt: When is a Lift Plan required?
options: For every lift, regardless of category
quiz.explanation: A Lift Plan is required for every lift.

quiz.prompt: Underground storage tank installation is usually …
quiz.explanation: UST installation is listed as Category 2 in 04.100.

lessons.title: Goal Zero, the Life-Saving Rules and Start Work Checks
body: Our target is Goal Zero: no harm to people and no significant incidents. We get there through honesty, integrity and respect for people, and by changing how we think and act. Four sets of enablers support Goal Zero: the Shell Golden Rules, the Life-Saving Rules, Start Work Checks and the Artelia Safety Rules.

The Golden Rules: comply with the law, standards and procedures; intervene on unsafe conditions or non-compliant actions; and respect our neighbours. Where a national law sets an even higher requirement, we meet the national requirement.

The nine Life-Saving Rules are the same across Shell. Bypassing safety controls: get authorisation before overriding or disabling safety-critical equipment such as alarms and sensors, deviating from a procedure or crossing a barrier. Confined space: get authorisation before entering; confirm energy is isolated, the atmosphere is tested and monitored, breathing apparatus is checked when required, an attendant is standing by and a rescue plan is in place. Driving: always wear a seat belt, keep within the speed limit and slow down for road conditions, do not use a phone while driving, be fit and rested, and follow journey management.

Energy isolation: verify isolation and zero energy before work begins — identify every energy source, isolate, lock and tag it (LOTO on electrical and fuel lines) and test for residual or stored energy. Hot work: control flammables and ignition sources, get authorisation, and in a hazardous area confirm a gas test has been done and gas is monitored continuously. Line of fire: keep yourself and others clear of moving objects, vehicles, pressure releases and dropped objects; obey barriers and exclusion zones and secure loose objects.

Safe mechanical lifting: confirm the equipment and load are inspected and fit for purpose, only operate equipment you are qualified for, and never walk under a suspended load. Work authorisation: work with a valid permit when required, understand it, confirm hazards are controlled, and stop and reassess if conditions change. Working at height: inspect fall protection before use, secure tools and materials, and tie off 100% to approved anchor points outside a protected area.

Compliance with the Life-Saving Rules is mandatory for everyone on Shell business and Shell sites. Breaking a rule, or encouraging or tolerating rule-breaking, leads to disciplinary action: if you choose to break the rules, you choose not to work for Shell. Every reported breach is investigated thoroughly and fairly.

Start Work Checks are a tool for putting the Life-Saving Rules into practice. The person doing the work confirms, just before starting, that the life-saving controls and safeguards are in place, and a verifier confirms it too (dual assurance). There are 13 activity-based checks, for example confined space, driving, energy isolation, hot work, lifting, working at height, excavation and live electrical work. They move us from "I stop work when I see a problem" to "I confirm the safeguards before I start".

Artelia Safety Rules: always have the mandatory PPE — helmet, safety shoes, safety vest and work clothes — and carry gloves and goggles. Use extra PPE when the task needs it, and double hearing protection above 95 dBA. Be trained and competent, do your last minute risk assessment, use the right tools, follow procedures and the JHA, protect your work area and keep it tidy. Report all hazards and incidents; an injured person going to a doctor must always be accompanied, and Artelia must be informed. Never smoke on site, never work intoxicated, avoid your phone while working, and stop work whenever you feel unsafe. HSSE is everyone's responsibility.
keyPoints: Goal Zero: no harm to people, no significant incidents
Nine Life-Saving Rules — compliance is mandatory
Get authorisation before bypassing safety controls
Verify isolation and zero energy before work
Never walk under a suspended load
Tie off 100% when working at height
Start Work Checks: confirm safeguards before you start, with a verifier
Double hearing protection above 95 dBA
Stop work whenever you feel unsafe

quiz.prompt: What does Goal Zero mean?
options: No harm to people and no significant incidents
Zero permits raised in a month
Zero cost overruns on a project
quiz.explanation: Goal Zero means no harm to people and no significant incidents.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four enablers of Goal Zero described in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: The enablers are the Golden Rules, the Life-Saving Rules, Start Work Checks and the Artelia Safety Rules.

quiz.prompt: A national law sets a higher safety requirement than the Shell procedure. What do you do?
quiz.explanation: If national law requires a higher level of compliance, we meet that national requirement.

quiz.prompt: You need to disable a station alarm or sensor to do your work. What must you do first?
options: Nothing, if it is only for a short time
Obtain authorisation before overriding or disabling it
quiz.explanation: Life-Saving Rule: obtain authorisation before overriding or disabling safety controls.

quiz.prompt: Which of these must be in place before entering a confined space?
options: A second person inside with you, nobody outside
Only a torch and a helmet
Nothing if the entry is under 5 minutes
Energy isolated, atmosphere tested and monitored, an attendant standing by and a rescue plan
quiz.explanation: Confirm isolation, gas testing and monitoring, an attendant and a rescue plan, and get authorisation to enter.

quiz.prompt: What does the energy isolation rule require before work begins?
options: Verify isolation and zero energy, including residual or stored energy
Ask the station manager if it is off
Switch the equipment off at the panel
Wear rubber gloves instead of isolating
quiz.explanation: Isolate, lock and tag every energy source (LOTO) and test that there is zero energy before starting.

quiz.prompt: Under the safe mechanical lifting rule, who may walk under a suspended load?
quiz.explanation: No one is allowed to walk under a suspended load.

quiz.prompt: When working at height outside a protected area, how must you be tied off?
options: Tying off is optional above 2 m
100% of the time to an approved anchor point
quiz.explanation: Tie off 100% to approved anchor points while outside a protected area.

quiz.prompt: What is the main purpose of a Start Work Check?
options: To confirm the life-saving controls and safeguards are in place just before work starts, with a verifier
To replace the permit to work
quiz.explanation: Start Work Checks are a last verification, with dual assurance, that safeguards are in place before work begins. They supplement, not replace, the permit system.

quiz.prompt: Under the Artelia Safety Rules, when must you use double hearing protection?
quiz.explanation: Use dual hearing protection where noise exceeds 95 dBA.

lessons.title: Permit to Work: PTW, JHA and WCF, and building a risk assessment
body: The retail Permit to Work (PTW) system sits under work authorisation and uses three documents: the Permit to Work, the Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) and the Work Clearance Form (WCF).

Permit to Work: keep a copy with all its attachments at the work site. It records the work site details, the permit issuer, when the permit is valid, the activities it covers, who isolates equipment before work and who recommissions it afterwards, emergency contacts, any additional hazards and controls not covered in the WCF and JHA, other attached documents (JHA, gas test records, licences), and the signatures of the permit holder and the permit issuer.

Job Hazard Analysis: records the station, which activities the work involves, a reference and review number, the work description and expected duration, the PPE to be used throughout, the equipment needed such as fire extinguishers and barricades, and the work crew's acknowledgement.

Work Clearance Form: records the job and site information, the minimum PPE, the Life-Saving Rules that apply, the work description, the risk level (high, medium or other), the permit number and JHA reference, the hazards and controls including tools and equipment, and where the fire extinguishers are. It is acknowledged by the contractor, the work crew and the site representative, and closed out by the contractor and the site representative. Do your last minute risk assessment before and during every task.

Which documents you need is set by Appendix 2 of the retail PTW activity table. High-risk activities (for example hot work or confined space entry) need all three: WCF, JHA and Permit to Work. Medium-risk activities need the WCF and the JHA. All other work needs the WCF only. A permit is just paper unless it is discussed with the team — paper cannot save your life.

A risk assessment has four main steps: select the job, break it into a sequence of steps, identify the hazards in each step, and decide the controls. The JHA/risk assessment shows the assessment number, contractor, site, date, work description, minimum PPE, work equipment and a risk rating matrix, which rates each risk by severity and likelihood so the biggest risks get attention first. When it is a full risk assessment, also record who might be harmed and the risk rating before and after controls. If the scope, conditions, procedure or equipment change, the permit issuer or permit holder amends the assessment and the crew signs again.

Major hazard types: contact hazards (struck by or against, cuts, falling objects, caught in or between); falls (slips, trips, falls on the same level and from height); strains and over-exertion (lifting, pushing, pulling, bending, twisting); exposure (extreme temperatures, chemical burns, radiation, hazardous atmospheres, noise); and energy sources (electricity, pressure, compression and tension).

Controls should bring each hazard down to an acceptable level, in this order: eliminate the hazard (change the process, use safer equipment or another method); if not possible, isolate it (barriers, guards, segregating the area); and if neither is possible, minimise it (less hazardous materials, PPE, safe work procedures, training and regular inspection).
keyPoints: Three PTW documents: Permit to Work, JHA, WCF
High risk = WCF + JHA + PTW
Medium risk = WCF + JHA
Other work = WCF only
Risk assessment: select job, break into steps, find hazards, decide controls
Risk matrix = severity × likelihood
Controls in order: eliminate, isolate, minimise
A permit is just paper unless discussed with the team

quiz.prompt: What are the three documents of the retail Permit to Work system?
options: Permit to Work, Job Hazard Analysis and Work Clearance Form
Gas test record, licence and ID card
Timesheet, PPE log and toolbox register
quiz.explanation: The PTW system uses the Permit to Work, the JHA and the WCF.

quiz.prompt: Which documents does a HIGH-risk activity such as hot work need?
options: WCF, JHA and Permit to Work
quiz.explanation: High-risk activities require all three PTW documents.

quiz.prompt: Which documents does a MEDIUM-risk activity need?
quiz.explanation: Medium-risk activities need the Work Clearance Form and the Job Hazard Analysis.

quiz.prompt: Where must the Permit to Work and its attachments be kept during the job?
quiz.explanation: Always have a copy of the permit and its attachments ready at the work site.

quiz.prompt: What are the four main steps of a risk assessment?
options: Select the job, break it into steps, identify hazards, determine controls
quiz.explanation: Select the job, break it into a sequence of steps, identify hazards and determine controls.

quiz.prompt: A risk rating matrix rates each risk by…
quiz.explanation: The matrix assesses severity and likelihood to prioritise risks.

quiz.prompt: What is the most effective way to control a hazard?
quiz.explanation: Elimination comes first, then isolation, then minimisation (including PPE).

quiz.prompt: The job scope changes halfway through. What happens to the JHA / risk assessment?
options: It is amended and the crew signs again
quiz.explanation: Amend the risk assessment and sign off if scope, conditions, procedure or equipment change.

quiz.prompt: Lifting, pushing, pulling, bending and twisting belong to which hazard group?
quiz.explanation: These are strain and over-exertion hazards.

quiz.prompt: "A permit is merely a paper if not discussed with the team." What does this mean?
options: Only the supervisor needs to read it
The permit only protects people if its hazards and controls are discussed and understood by the crew
quiz.explanation: A paper cannot save your life — the team must discuss and understand the permit.

lessons.title: Hazardous zones, fire prevention and firefighting
body: Every retail site selling fuel and gas has a Hazardous Areas map. It highlights the petrol dispensers (high fire risk from fuel handling), the oil–water separators (to prevent contamination from spills) and the LPG dispensers. Any hot work inside these hazardous areas needs a Permit to Work.

Hazardous areas are classified into three zones. Zone 0: an explosive atmosphere of air mixed with flammable gas, vapour or mist is present. Zone 1: an explosive atmosphere is likely to occur occasionally during normal activities. Zone 2: an explosive atmosphere is not expected in normal operation, and if it does occur it lasts only a short time.

Sources of ignition include hot surfaces (exhausts, machinery), electrostatic discharge, open flames and hot gases, electrical equipment such as switches and motors that can spark, stray electricity and lightning, radio-frequency and electromagnetic waves, ionising radiation, and adiabatic compression from rapid pressure changes or shock waves.

Fire prevention means acting before a fire starts: regularly checking and fixing electrical systems, heating devices and fire alarms, and teaching people about fire safety. Fire can injure and kill, and careless actions can start one, so we all have to be responsible.
The fire triangle: a fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen together. Remove any one of the three and the fire goes out.

Fire precautions: install smoke detectors, heat detectors and fire alarms; keep escape routes clear and well lit, with doors that open easily; place the right type of fire extinguisher at strategic points; and train everyone on alarms, evacuation and using fire equipment.

Means of firefighting: sand smothers fires in solids such as wood and paper; water cools fires in paper, wood and other solids; CO2 is effective on flammable liquids, gases and electrical equipment; foam forms a layer that keeps oxygen away from burning liquids; dry powder works on many types of fire.

In a fire: stay calm, alert others and call the fire brigade immediately, close doors and windows to slow the fire and smoke, and evacuate using the designated exit routes to the assembly point. Only try to put out a fire if you are trained and have the correct extinguisher — otherwise, getting people out of danger is the safer choice.
keyPoints: Hot work in a hazardous area needs a Permit to Work
Zone 0, Zone 1, Zone 2 — Zone 0 is the most hazardous
Fire triangle: heat, fuel, oxygen — remove one to stop the fire
Keep escape routes clear and well lit
CO2 or foam for flammable liquids; CO2 for electrical equipment
Stay calm, raise the alarm, call the fire brigade, evacuate
Only fight a fire if trained and with the right extinguisher

quiz.prompt: What must you have before doing hot work inside a site's hazardous area?
options: Nothing if it takes under 10 minutes
A verbal OK from a colleague
quiz.explanation: Any hot work within the hazardous areas requires a Permit to Work.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is normally marked on a retail site Hazardous Areas map?
options: Petrol dispensers, oil–water separators and LPG dispensers
quiz.explanation: The map highlights petrol dispensers, oil–water separators and LPG dispensers.

quiz.prompt: In which zone is an explosive atmosphere NOT expected in normal operation, and lasts only a short time if it does occur?
quiz.explanation: Zone 2: not expected in normal operation; if it occurs, only for a short duration.

quiz.prompt: Which of these can be a source of ignition?
options: A switch or motor that sparks
quiz.explanation: Electrostatic discharge, electrical equipment and hot surfaces are all ignition sources.

quiz.prompt: What are the three elements of the fire triangle?
quiz.explanation: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen; removing any one extinguishes it.

quiz.prompt: Which extinguishing agent is suitable for a fire in electrical equipment?
quiz.explanation: CO2 is effective on flammable liquids, gases and electrical equipment.

quiz.prompt: How does firefighting foam put out a flammable liquid fire?
options: It forms a layer that stops the fuel touching oxygen
It only cools the air above the fire
quiz.explanation: Foam forms a barrier between the fuel and oxygen.

quiz.prompt: A fire breaks out and you have not been trained to use the extinguisher. What should you do?
options: Raise the alarm, call the fire brigade and evacuate by the designated route
Open all windows to clear the smoke
quiz.explanation: Only fight a fire if trained and with the right extinguisher; otherwise alert others, call the fire brigade and evacuate.

quiz.prompt: Why should you close doors and windows as you leave a fire?
options: To contain the fire and slow the spread of smoke, giving more time to evacuate
quiz.explanation: Closing doors and windows helps contain the fire and limit smoke spread.

lessons.title: Safe working area, plant and equipment, manual handling and safe behaviour
body: Working areas must be clearly segregated — safe walkways and green zones apart from restricted areas such as excavations, open manholes, storage and lifting areas — using the correct barriers. Good signage with pictograms and caution notices in the local language tells people about the hazards and the main site rules.

Slips, trips and falls injure many people every year and are mostly preventable. They come from poor housekeeping: tools, debris, cables or materials left on the ground, spills not cleaned up, mud and wet patches, poor lighting, and missing barriers or signs. Prevent them by clearing waste as it is produced, bundling or bagging light waste, removing nails from scrap timber, cleaning spills straight away, routing power-tool cables above head height where possible, cleaning muddy boots before climbing ladders, keeping work areas well lit and putting up barricades and signs.

Most plant and equipment accidents come from wrong use — being trained and competent is the key. With abrasive wheels: never exceed the maximum speed, don't press hard or use the side of the wheel, keep fingers clear, and wear the right PPE including ear and full-face protection. For portable grinders: only mount a wheel if you are trained, use the correct disc, check the maximum speed on both the wheel and the tool, adjust the guard to expose as little wheel as possible, and watch out for people around you.

For bench-mounted wheels: put the glass screen in the safe position, wear eye and ear protection, keep fingers below the tool-rest level, use cut-resistant gloves and a push stick on table saws, and cover blades when you finish. After replacing a wheel, test-run it for at least one minute. Stop the wheel when not in use and switch off the power when equipment is idle or left unattended.

Manual handling — lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling and carrying — is involved in nearly 30% of incidents: get it wrong today and you suffer tomorrow. Avoid manual handling by using machines where possible. When you must lift, use the kinetic technique: bend your knees, grasp the load, lift with your legs, then carry. Use aids such as lifting platforms, hand hooks and rollers, and team-lift heavy loads to share the weight.

Good housekeeping is part of HSSE. In waste management, prevention is the most preferred option and disposal the least preferred. Keep contaminated waste in a separate covered metal bin and dispose of it through approved waste contractors.

More than 90% of injuries result from risky behaviour. Behaviour is what people do that others can see, shaped by culture, education and values. Before any work: identify the hazards, put the controls in place, get the permits, follow the job procedure, and stop the work if hazards are not under control. Your actions silently influence others — be a safety ambassador and set the example for your team.
keyPoints: Segregate work areas with proper barriers and signs in the local language
Most slips, trips and falls come from poor housekeeping
Never exceed an abrasive wheel's maximum speed
Test-run a new wheel for at least one minute
Lift with your legs: bend knees, grasp, lift, carry
Waste: prevention first, disposal last
Over 90% of injuries come from risky behaviour — lead by example

quiz.prompt: What is the most common cause of slips, trips and falls on site?
options: Poor housekeeping — items, spills and mud left on the ground
quiz.explanation: Slips, trips and falls are mostly caused by poor housekeeping.

quiz.prompt: Where should power-tool cables be routed when possible?
quiz.explanation: Route cables above head height whenever possible to prevent trips.

quiz.prompt: Which is correct when using an abrasive wheel?
options: Never exceed the maximum speed marked on the wheel and the tool
Use the side of the wheel for faster cutting
Remove the guard for a better view
quiz.explanation: Never exceed the maximum speed; use the correct disc and keep the guard adjusted.

quiz.prompt: After replacing a wheel on a bench grinder, what should you do?
options: Run it only at half speed forever
Test-run it for at least one minute
quiz.explanation: Run a test for at least one minute to check for irregularities.

quiz.prompt: Roughly what share of incidents involve manual handling?
quiz.explanation: Manual handling is involved in nearly 30% of incidents.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct order for a safe (kinetic) lift?
options: Pull the load towards you with your arms only
Bend your back, grab, twist, carry
Bend your knees, grasp the load, lift using your legs, carry
quiz.explanation: Bend the knees, grasp the load, lift with the legs, then carry.

quiz.prompt: In waste management, which is the MOST preferred option?
quiz.explanation: Prevention is the most preferred option; disposal the least preferred.

quiz.prompt: How should contaminated waste be kept?
options: In a separate covered metal bin, disposed of through an approved waste contractor
In an open pile at the back of the site
quiz.explanation: Keep contaminated waste in a separate covered metal bin and use approved waste contractors.

quiz.prompt: What share of injuries result from risky behaviour?
quiz.explanation: More than 90% of injuries result from risky behaviours.

lessons.title: Major hazardous activities: height, scaffolds, lifting, pressure, electricity, substances and PPE
body: Major hazardous activities include handling chemicals, operating heavy machinery, working at height, heat and cold exposure (prevent with suitable clothing, drinking water and rest breaks) and transporting hazardous materials.

Working at height means working 1.8 m or more above the ground. Before you start, ask: what is the job and its risks, what is my part, how high and in what conditions (weather, light), is it planned and prepared, are we communicating, is there enough working space, do we have the right tools and materials, do I have the right personal and collective protective equipment (PPE and CPE), and what did my last minute risk assessment show?

Ladders: a straight standing ladder is for access only — going up or down — not for working from. Platform ladders and A-frame ladders are approved for work at height, but avoid working from ladders where a scaffold or work platform can be used. Inspect ladders for missing or loose rungs; do not use painted ladders (paint hides damage); label and remove defective ladders and never repair them yourself. On an A-frame, keep off the top three rungs and have a buddy hold it from outside the line of fire. Set ladders on firm, level, non-slip ground at 75° (1 out for every 4 up), tie them at the top (or secure the bottom if the top can't be tied), extend them 1 m above the landing, face the ladder, hold with both hands and never over-reach. Don't stand them on drums or boxes, don't carry heavy loads up (use a hoist), and keep metal ladders away from electrical hazards. Most ladder accidents happen because the ladder was not secured at the top.

Case study: a worker pushing a long metal rod through a wall touched a 4,800-volt power line and was electrocuted. Survey the site for hazards during planning, train workers in their own language, and give scaffold workers training from a qualified person.

Scaffolds: mobile towers on wheels and fixed scaffolds. Steel mobile scaffolds are banned on Shell retail sites — use standard aluminium mobile towers. Only a competent person may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold. Fixed scaffolds must be tied to the structure; every scaffold and platform must show its safe working load; nobody stays on a tower while it is moved; check wheels and brakes. Tube-and-fitting scaffolds are built from tubes, fittings (clamps) and couplers. Never climb the tubes — use the ladder; keep a 60 cm passage clear when stacking materials; don't leave tools lying about; fit guard rails and toe boards wherever someone could fall; never use an incomplete scaffold or remove ties, rails, braces, toe boards or ladders; never throw or drop materials. The scaffold should be no more than 20 cm from the structure, with at least 60 cm working space.

MEWPs (mobile elevating work platforms) are for short tasks. Inspect and test them before each use, wear a fall-arrest harness clipped to the anchor points in the manual, and only trained, certified people may operate them. On roofs: competent workers only, guard rails and toe boards before work starts, harnesses with suitable anchors, a clear work area, safety nets where needed and regular equipment checks. Check the competence of any supplier who repairs or maintains your fall protection equipment.

Lifting and hoisting: dropped objects cause injuries, deaths and damage. Every critical lift is controlled by a permit. The permit issuer checks the lifting equipment is suitable and its safety devices work. The rigging supervisor makes sure the equipment matches the lift plan, the controls and lift procedure are followed, people are kept clear of loads, and a flagman is assigned when cranes move near overhead lines or among people and plant. Riggers use standard signals and taglines and stay out of the line of fire. Crane operators and anyone needing tight-fitting respiratory protection must hold a fitness-to-work certificate before starting.

Pressure (air, hydraulics, pneumatic tools, jacks) can kill when released. Never open equipment that is under pressure; both sides of every connection must have the same diameter, make and thread; check hammer unions with go/no-go rings; use flashback arresters. Causes of pressure incidents include not following procedures, mismatched connections, damaged hoses, not depressurising or isolating (LOTO), failed valves and fittings, trusting faulty gauges and transferring from high- to low-pressure systems. Control it with the right equipment, barriers and buffer zones, working gauges and relief valves, communication before opening valves, secured temporary piping, permits and trained workers.

Electricity gives no warning. Before digging, check the utility plans, use a cable locator you are trained on, assume every cable is live, hand-dig trial holes and look for marker tape or tiles. Treat all overhead lines as live — never assume they are telephone cables — keep the clearance distances set by the Oman electricity standards, check for overhead lines before moving scaffolds or ladders, and never stack materials under them.

Hazardous substances can be corrosive, dangerous to the environment, explosive, very toxic, oxidising, harmful or irritant, or highly flammable (like petrol and solvents). They enter the body by swallowing, breathing in, or absorption through skin and eyes. On site you may meet contaminated ground, solvent fumes, epoxy paints, concrete admixtures, hardwood dust, welding fumes, cement, resins and asbestos in old buildings. Assess the risk first — can the substance be eliminated or replaced with something safer? Read the safety data sheet, be trained, wear gloves, goggles, respirators or chemical suits as needed, know where the first aid kit and washing facilities are, store substances securely below head height after use, never eat, drink or smoke while handling them, and wash your hands.

PPE is the gear and clothing that protects you at work. Some PPE is preventive (high-visibility vests, positioning systems); some reduces the consequences when something goes wrong (hard hats, full-body harnesses). PPE must meet the recognised standards and local regulations — for example, safety helmets, steel-toe safety shoes, safety glasses, ear defenders or earplugs, cut-resistant gloves, Class II high-visibility vests and disposable FFP respirators. Ask Artelia HSSE or your project manager for the standards for other equipment.
keyPoints: Work at height = 1.8 m or more
Straight ladders are for access only; 75° angle, tied at the top, 1 m above the landing
Keep off the top three rungs of an A-frame ladder
Steel mobile scaffolds are banned on Shell retail sites
Only a competent person erects or alters a scaffold
Every critical lift needs a permit; stay out from under loads
Never open equipment under pressure; match every connection
Treat every cable and overhead line as live
Read the safety data sheet before using a hazardous substance

quiz.prompt: From what height is work considered 'working at height' in this course?
quiz.explanation: Working at height means work at 1.8 m and above.

quiz.prompt: What is a straight standing (lean-to) ladder allowed to be used for?
options: As a work platform for painting
Access only — going up or down
quiz.explanation: Access ladders must not be used as work platforms.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct angle for a leaning ladder?
quiz.explanation: Set ladders at 75°: one unit out for every four units up.

quiz.prompt: Why should you not use a heavily painted ladder?
quiz.explanation: Paint can hide damaged parts that make the ladder unsafe.

quiz.prompt: Which type of mobile scaffold is banned on Shell retail sites?
quiz.explanation: Steel mobile scaffolds are banned; standard aluminium towers are used.

quiz.prompt: Who may erect, alter or dismantle a scaffold?
quiz.explanation: Scaffold erection, alteration and dismantling is a specialist job for a competent person.

quiz.prompt: A mobile scaffold tower needs to be moved. What about the people on it?
options: Nobody may be on it while it is moved
They can stay on if they hold on
quiz.explanation: When the tower is moved there must never be anyone on it.

quiz.prompt: What controls a critical lift?
options: Nothing if the crane is new
quiz.explanation: Any critical lift has to be controlled using a permit.

quiz.prompt: Which is a common cause of pressure incidents?
options: Using mismatched connections or not depressurising before work
Using connections with matching diameter and thread
quiz.explanation: Mismatched connections and failure to depressurise or isolate are major causes.

quiz.prompt: Before digging, how should you treat underground cables?
options: Assume all cables are live unless proven isolated, and locate them first
Only check if you see a sign
quiz.explanation: Check plans, use a cable locator, assume all cables are live and hand-dig trial holes.

quiz.prompt: How can a hazardous substance enter your body?
options: Swallowing, breathing it in, or absorption through skin and eyes
quiz.explanation: Ingestion, inhalation and absorption are the three routes.

quiz.prompt: Where do you find the hazards, safe handling and emergency information for a chemical?
quiz.explanation: The material safety data sheet has the hazards, safe handling and emergency measures.

lessons.title: Near misses, LMRA, Talk Not Tick, emergency response and first aid
body: Know the difference. A potential incident is an unsafe condition, act or omission that could cause injury or damage; depending on how serious the outcome could be, it may be raised to a high-potential incident. A near miss is when something unsafe happens but nobody is hurt — it almost caused harm. An incident is an event where real harm or damage occurs; it is investigated and actions are taken so it does not happen again. Potential incidents and near misses that are stopped and reported to the site supervisor in time prevent injuries, damage and losses.

Report near misses and potential incidents on the reporting form: site, date, place, time, type, what happened, the immediate action taken and recommendations. Every contractor's HSSE Focal reports NMPIs to Artelia on the digital platform. The Artelia retail contractor incident procedure covers personal injuries, loss of primary containment (LOPC) above 100 kg (120 L), Life-Saving Rule violations and high-potential incidents; significant incidents such as fatalities have extra reporting and investigation requirements. First aid cases, near misses, potential incidents and LOPCs below 100 kg with no serious consequence do not need a formal investigation, but the local HSSE manager and contract holder may decide to investigate.

Last Minute Risk Assessment (LMRA): after the start-work discussion or toolbox talk, everyone does their own LMRA. Check for accidental energy release (flow, pressure, electricity, chemical, potential, rotating and kinetic energy); the right PPE; the right tools — a complete set, power tools on an earth-leakage breaker, ATEX-certified tools in hazardous zones, industrial plugs and sockets, and cords that are not a trip hazard; and your position — falling into excavations or pits, falls from height, line of fire and hazards from contractors working nearby. However many times you have done the job, do an LMRA before every task.

Talk Not Tick (TNT) is a conversation, not a tick-box exercise. Talking with people who are exposed to unsafe conditions or doing unsafe acts — rather than just filing a complaint — changes behaviour. It is positive, engages people, is measurable and rewarding. Once agreement is reached after the intervention, the supervisor records it on the TNT form (site, date, people involved and what was discussed).

Emergency response, step 1 — immediate response: notify the site supervisor or site manager first; as on-scene commander they start the emergency response and notifications. Look after the injured and call emergency services if needed. Anyone needing medical attention must always be accompanied off site. Tell the site operator if the station is open.

Step 2 — notification: whatever the severity, phone the Artelia project manager within one hour of the incident — even for a minor first aid case or when not all details are known. The written report can follow later. Emergency contact numbers must be displayed at every site.

Incidents include injuries, fires, damage to power cables or gas and water mains, petroleum leaks and spills, finding oil or contaminated soil, chemical incidents, accidents involving the public or vehicles, crane overturns and the collapse of structures, slopes, ladders or scaffolds. Also: keep everyone calm, photograph or sketch the scene, take witness details, do not restart work until it is completely safe, keep copies of logbooks, the WCF, JHA and PTW, share the lessons learned while respecting the privacy of those hurt, and keep emergency numbers to hand.

Every team must have a certified first aider. First aid priorities: save life, stop injuries getting worse, and get the person to medical help quickly — always accompanied. A site needs a first aid kit suited to the number of people and the work, plus items such as a fire blanket, eye wash and stretcher. Do not leave the casualty; send someone for help; always wear gloves to avoid cross-contamination.
keyPoints: Near miss: something unsafe happened, nobody was hurt
Potential incident: an unsafe act or condition that could cause harm
Do an LMRA before every task, however experienced you are
Talk Not Tick: have the conversation, then record it
Tell the site supervisor first
Phone the Artelia project manager within 1 hour of any incident
Injured people always go to medical care accompanied
Every team needs a certified first aider

quiz.prompt: A hose bursts near a worker but nobody is hurt. What is this?
options: A potential incident only if someone saw it
quiz.explanation: A near miss is when something unsafe happens but no harm occurs.

quiz.prompt: A damaged ladder is left on site and nobody has used it yet. What is this?
quiz.explanation: Unsafe conditions, acts or omissions that could cause harm are potential incidents.

quiz.prompt: When must you do a Last Minute Risk Assessment?
options: Before every task, however many times you have done it
quiz.explanation: Before each task we must do an LMRA, regardless of experience.

quiz.prompt: Which tools are required for use in hazardous zones?
quiz.explanation: The LMRA checks for ATEX-certified tools in hazardous zones.

quiz.prompt: What is Talk Not Tick (TNT)?
options: A checklist you tick without talking
A conversation with people exposed to unsafe acts or conditions, rather than a tick-box exercise
quiz.explanation: TNT is an outcomes-led conversation to improve behavioural safety; the supervisor records it afterwards.

quiz.prompt: Who should be notified first of any incident or near miss on site?
options: The site supervisor or site manager
Nobody until the end of the shift
quiz.explanation: The site supervisor or manager is notified first and acts as on-scene commander.

quiz.prompt: Within what time must the Artelia project manager be phoned about an incident?
options: At the end of the month
quiz.explanation: Notify the Artelia project manager by phone within a maximum of one hour, even for minor first aid cases.

quiz.prompt: A worker needs to see a doctor after an injury. How should they leave site?
quiz.explanation: Anyone needing medical attention must always be accompanied.

quiz.prompt: What are the priorities of first aid?
options: Save life, prevent the injury getting worse and get the person to medical help promptly
Move the casualty to the office
quiz.explanation: First aid priorities: save lives, prevent worsening and evacuate promptly to medical help.

quiz.prompt: Why should you wear gloves when giving first aid?
quiz.explanation: Always wear gloves to prevent cross-contamination.

lessons.title: Promoting HSSE on site, awards and the assessment
body: Promoting HSSE (health, safety, security and environment) means actively putting the wellbeing of people and the environment first. It means showing the benefits of working safely, reducing the downsides of unsafe work by dealing with hazards and risks, and making everyone aware of what unsafe work leads to. Strong systems and procedures should make unsafe working practically impossible and build a culture of safety and security.
Strong basic safety rules are absolute: they do not change, they are not negotiable and they are not open to discussion. They apply to everyone, without exception.

Good safety is recognised. Shell gives annual awards — cash, certificates and recognition — to frontline workers, line managers and supervisors in categories such as HSSE initiative, worker, operator or driver, emergency response, core team and contractor. Artelia also runs a monthly programme: a Safety Champion of the month is chosen for Near Miss and Potential Incident (NMPI) reports, interventions and responsible safe behaviour, and receives a cash or gift reward, a certificate and team appreciation. Supervisors and safety officers are also recognised every quarter.

You are free to choose, but you are not free from the consequences of your choice — think before you act. And if there's any doubt, get it out: never carry on working with uncertainty when your actions can affect everyone's safety.
To receive the Safety Passport card you must pass the Safety Passport assessment with at least 80%.
keyPoints: HSSE = health, safety, security and environment
Make unsafe working practically impossible
Basic safety rules are absolute and apply to everyone
Artelia names a Safety Champion every month
If there's any doubt, get it out
Pass mark for the Safety Passport: 80%

quiz.prompt: What does HSSE stand for?
quiz.explanation: HSSE stands for health, safety, security and environment.

quiz.prompt: How are strong basic safety rules described?
options: Suggestions that are open to discussion
Absolute, unchanging and non-negotiable, applying to everyone without exception
Guidelines that supervisors can relax when work is urgent
quiz.explanation: Basic safety rules are absolute and non-negotiable, and apply to everyone.

quiz.prompt: What is the Artelia Safety Champion of the month chosen for?
options: Having the longest time with the company
Near Miss / Potential Incident reports, interventions and responsible safe behaviour
quiz.explanation: The monthly Safety Champion is selected on NMPIs reported, interventions done and responsible safe behaviour.

quiz.prompt: How often are supervisors and safety officers recognised by Artelia, in addition to the monthly champion?
quiz.explanation: Supervisors and safety officers are rewarded and recognised quarterly.

quiz.prompt: You are unsure whether a job is safe to continue. What does "If there's any doubt, get it out" tell you to do?
options: Clear the doubt before continuing — do not work with uncertainty
quiz.explanation: Working with uncertainty where safety is at stake must be avoided; resolve the doubt first.

quiz.prompt: What score do you need in the Safety Passport assessment to receive the card?
quiz.explanation: The Safety Passport exam pass mark is 80%.

summary: Electrical Safety Rules for retail sites: roles (CEP / AP), isolation and lock-out, proving dead, hazardous-area equipment and safe working distances.

title: Confined Space Entry
summary: Entering tanks, chambers and interceptors safely: identifying confined spaces, the entry permit, continuous gas monitoring, attendants, and rescue planning.

summary: Inspecting scaffolds and mobile towers before use (tags, base, ties, guardrails, access) and planning and practising rescue from height.
